reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO
clinicalPearls: Caused by the intracellular bacterium Coxiella burnetii, acquired mainly by inhaling aerosols from infected livestock, particularly around parturition, birth fluids, and contaminated dust
Occupational exposure (farmers, abattoir workers, veterinarians) and even wind-borne spread from farms are important epidemiological clues
Acute Q fever is frequently a self-limiting flu-like illness, but can present as atypical pneumonia or as granulomatous hepatitis with fever
The organism is highly resistant in the environment and remarkably infectious at very low doses
Chronic Q fever, developing months to years later, most often manifests as culture-negative endocarditis, especially in those with pre-existing valve disease, prosthetic valves, or vascular grafts
Diagnosis is largely serological using phase I and phase II antibodies: phase II dominance suggests acute disease and high phase I titres point to chronic infection
Treatment of acute disease relies on a tetracycline-class agent, whereas chronic endocarditis requires prolonged combination therapy and long-term follow-up
reference.pathophysiology: Coxiella burnetii is an obligate intracellular Gram-negative bacterium that survives as a hardy spore-like form in the environment. After inhalation it is taken up by alveolar macrophages and replicates within acidified phagolysosomes, disseminating to liver, lung, and other organs and provoking granulomatous inflammation. It undergoes antigenic phase variation, which underlies the serological distinction between acute and chronic infection. In chronic disease the organism persists at sites such as damaged or prosthetic heart valves and vascular tissue, driving endovascular infection.
additionalDifferentials: Viral hepatitis and other causes of granulomatous hepatitis
Infective endocarditis from other culture-negative organisms (for chronic disease)
Influenza and other viral febrile illnesses
additionalInvestigations: Phase I and phase II serology (immunofluorescence) as the mainstay, interpreted for acute versus chronic pattern
PCR for Coxiella DNA in early acute infection before antibodies rise
Liver function tests and, where relevant, liver biopsy showing characteristic granulomas
Echocardiography and vascular imaging when chronic Q fever or endocarditis is suspected
redFlags: Persistent or relapsing fever with high phase I antibody titres suggesting chronic infection
New or changing murmur, embolic events, or heart failure indicating endocarditis
Fever in a patient with a prosthetic valve or vascular graft and compatible exposure
Q fever in pregnancy, which carries risks of chronic infection and adverse fetal outcomes
reference.prognosis: Acute Q fever usually resolves, often even without treatment, whereas chronic Q fever endocarditis is a serious condition requiring prolonged therapy and carries appreciable morbidity and mortality if not recognised and adequately treated.
pitfalls: Failing to take an occupational or animal-contact history in an atypical pneumonia or unexplained hepatitis
Labelling endocarditis as culture-negative without serological testing for Coxiella
Stopping therapy too early in chronic disease, risking relapse
Not screening or offering prophylaxis considerations to high-risk patients with valvulopathy after exposure
management: Treat acute Q fever with doxycycline as first-line therapy
Manage chronic Q fever endocarditis with prolonged combination doxycycline and hydroxychloroquine continued for many months to years
Use co-trimoxazole in pregnancy, where doxycycline is contraindicated, to reduce obstetric complications
Assess valves with echocardiography and consider valve or graft surgery for uncontrolled endovascular infection
Follow phase I and phase II serology after acute infection to detect progression to chronic disease, especially in those with valvular, prosthetic-valve or vascular-graft risk factors
Reduce exposure through occupational precautions and offer vaccination to high-risk groups such as abattoir workers
Refer to infectious diseases for guidance on prolonged therapy and monitoring

valueTables.title: CDC category A, B and C bioterrorism agents

cells.text: Anthrax (Bacillus anthracis); botulism (Clostridium botulinum toxin); plague (Yersinia pestis); smallpox (Variola major); tularemia (Francisella tularensis); viral hemorrhagic fevers: arenaviruses (Lassa, New World: Machupo, Junin, Guanarito and Sabia), Bunyaviridae (Crimean-Congo, Rift Valley), Filoviridae (Ebola, Marburg)

Brucellosis (Brucella spp.); epsilon toxin of Clostridium perfringens; food safety threats (for example Salmonella spp., Escherichia coli O157:H7, Shigella); glanders (Burkholderia mallei); melioidosis (B. pseudomallei); psittacosis (Chlamydophila psittaci); Q fever (Coxiella burnetii); ricin toxin from Ricinus communis (castor beans); staphylococcal enterotoxin B; typhus fever (Rickettsia prowazekii); viral encephalitis [alphaviruses, for example Venezuelan, eastern and western equine encephalitis]; water safety threats (for example Vibrio cholerae, Cryptosporidium parvum)
Emerging infectious disease threats such as Nipah, hantavirus, SARS coronavirus and pandemic influenza
